first_impression.reaction: Sophie here. I Googled this on my lunch break because Mum asked whether an Italian wedding would 'count' at home. The first line answered it straight away, and the second paragraph is what kept me reading: 'The harder questions start once you are home: you cannot register the marriage here, the certificate is in Italian, and a surname change is a separate application in several states.' I didn't know any of that. I'm a lawyer, so I read the legal section properly. James would read the takeaways and the surname bit and stop there.

journey.quote: Is marriage in Italy recognised in Australia? In most cases, yes: an overseas marriage is generally recognised here if it was valid where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law, according to both Smartraveller and the Attorney-General's Department.
journey.reaction: Straight answer, with sources named. No 'it depends, contact us to find out'. Good.

journey.quote: If you were born in Australia and want your partner's surname on your passport, the Passport Office always needs a name change certificate from an Australian registry.
journey.reaction: That's the one I'll forward to James and Mum. I would have assumed the Italian certificate was enough. This is exactly the kind of thing that bites you six months later at the passport counter.

journey.section: The legal test: what the Marriage Act says
journey.quote: Section 88D then says such a marriage "shall be recognised in Australia as valid", subject to a short list of exceptions.
journey.reaction: As a lawyer I like that they cite the actual section and the compilation date. James would glaze over here, but the 'For most couples none of this applies' line lets a skimmer move on, which is fair.

journey.section: Do you need to register an Italian marriage in Australia?
journey.quote: Before you leave Italy, ask for the comune's certificate, not the parish's.
journey.reaction: This is insider detail. James's family is Catholic and a church wedding has been floated. I had no idea the church act has to be transcribed by the comune to count.

journey.quote: The Australian Embassy in Rome advises using the Prefettura of the city where you marry, and warns appointments are hard to get from May to September.
journey.reaction: We're looking at a September wedding, so this is directly useful. It's the sort of thing I'd otherwise discover the day after the wedding with no one to call.

journey.quote: Not published: Prefettura processing times. Ask your Wedded Advisor to build the appointment into your plan.
journey.reaction: The 'Not published:' opener reads like someone's internal research note pasted into the article. Not published by whom? Fine once I work it out, but it's a bit clunky. Same with the multilingual extract line. I do like that the Advisor handles the appointment, but does that mean they book it, or just remind us?

journey.section: Travel in the name on your passport
journey.quote: Book the honeymoon in your current names and sort out the name change once home.
journey.reaction: Practical, specific, and one less thing to think about. This is what I want from a planner.

journey.section: Marry legally in Australia first, celebrate in Italy
journey.quote: You can sidestep most of this by signing the legal papers at home and keeping the Italian day for the vows, the dinner and the people.
journey.reaction: Honestly, after reading the paperwork sections this sounds like the sensible option for us. It's nice that they offer it rather than pushing everyone into the complicated route.

journey.section: The trade-offs if Italy should be 'the' wedding
journey.quote: The cost is emotional. Your legal anniversary becomes a short ceremony at home, and some couples feel the Italian vows repeat something already done.
journey.reaction: An honest trade-off, not a sales line. This is the conversation James and I would actually have. It makes me trust the rest of the article more.

journey.section: Get the legal side settled before you book
journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is one person from first idea to the last dance, working in your time zone and quoting in AUD, and confirms in writing what is included before you commit.
journey.reaction: AUD quotes and 'confirms in writing what is included' speak to my hidden-costs worry. But 'first idea to the last dance' is the same end-to-end promise every planner makes. What does that mean for the paperwork in this article? Do you handle the apostille and translation, or just tell us to?

unanswered_questions: Does the Wedded Advisor actually book the Prefettura apostille and arrange the NAATI translation for us, or do we do it ourselves with their reminders?
If we have a church wedding in Italy, does Wedded Wonderland follow up with the comune to make sure the act is transcribed?
Roughly what do the apostille, translation and an NSW change of name cost, and how long do they take?
If we marry legally in Sydney first, how close to the Italian date should we do it, and do most of your couples go that way?
Is there a real wedding we can look at where a couple married legally in Australia and held the celebration in Italy?
would_share_with: James (the Key takeaways and the surname section)
Mum, who asked whether an Italian wedding would count at home
James's parents, because of the church wedding and comune transcription point

cta_reaction.quote: When you are ready, speak with a Wedded Advisor about which route suits you.
cta_reaction.why: It's low-pressure, which I like, and choosing between legal-in-Italy and legal-at-home is a real question we have. But this is the first post I've read from them and we haven't picked a destination. I'd want to read another post or two and see a real wedding before I hand over our details.

top_3_changes: Rewrite the 'Not published:' lines as normal sentences (for example, 'The Prefettura doesn't publish processing times, so...') so they don't read like research notes.

Say plainly what the Wedded Advisor does on the paperwork in this article: book the Prefettura appointment, arrange the translation, check the comune transcription for a church wedding. That turns 'first idea to the last dance' into something I can believe.
Link to a real wedding (venue and date) where a couple married legally at home and celebrated in Italy, plus a line on when to do the Australian legal ceremony relative to the Italy trip.
